**Sūrat Saba'** (Sura of Sheba)

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Praise﴾: if it is taken as referring to the known (*al-ma'hūd*), then He is praised by what He praised Himself with. If it is taken as covering all (*al-istighrāq*, comprehensiveness), then He deserves the greater part of all praises.

﴿to God﴾, with the *lām* of ownership, because He is the Creator of the one who speaks praise at all. So by His ownership He is the owner of praise, and fit to be praised.

﴿to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, by creation, ownership and dominion. Therefore He is worthy of being praised openly and secretly.

﴿And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter﴾, just as it belongs to Him in this world, since blessings in both abodes come from the Master. However, praise is obligatory here, because this world is the abode of obligation, whereas there is no obligation there. The people of Paradise praise Him out of joy at the bounty and delight in the great reward they have obtained, by their saying: "Praise be to God, who has fulfilled His promise to us," and "Praise be to God, who has removed grief from us."

﴿And He is the All-Wise﴾, in governing whatever is in the heavens and the earth,

﴿the All-Aware﴾, knowing the inner thoughts of those who praise Him for the Day of Recompense and the Gathering.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 2:

﴿يَعْلَمُ﴾ ("He knows"): mustaʾnaf (a new, independent clause, not grammatically dependent on what precedes it).

﴿ما يَلِجُ﴾ ("what enters"): what enters.

﴿فِي الأرْضِ﴾ ("into the earth"): from the dead and the buried treasures.

﴿وَما يَخْرُجُ مِنها﴾ ("and what comes out of it"): from the plants and the precious substances of the minerals.

﴿وَما يَنْـزِلُ مِنَ السَماءِ﴾ ("and what descends from the sky"): from the rains and the various kinds of blessings.

﴿وَما يَعْرُجُ فِيها﴾ ("and what ascends into it"): what rises up to it from the angels and the supplications.

﴿وَهُوَ الرَحِيمُ﴾ ("and He is the Most Merciful"): by sending down what they need.

﴿الغَفُورُ﴾ ("the Most Forgiving"): toward what they dare to do against Him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 3:

﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, that is: those who deny the Resurrection,

﴿"The Hour will not come upon us."﴾ This is a negation of the Resurrection and a denial of the coming of the Hour.

﴿Say: "Yes, by my Lord."﴾ The word "bala" (بلى, "yes indeed") affirms what follows a negation, meaning that the matter is nothing but the Hour's coming.

﴿"By my Lord, it will surely come upon you."﴾ Then the affirmation is repeated, emphasized with that which is the utmost in emphasis and firmness, namely swearing by Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Then he reinforced the oath by the attribute that follows the one sworn by, in His words: ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾, because the greatness of the state of the one sworn by indicates the strength of the state of what is sworn to, and the firmness and steadfastness of it, for it is in the position of bearing witness to the matter. The more exalted the one witnessed by, the stronger and more certain the testimony, and the more firmly established the thing witnessed to. Since the establishment of the Hour is among the most prominent of the unseen matters, and the most hidden of them, the description by what pertains to knowledge of the unseen is more fitting and more appropriate.

"ʿĀlimu al-ghayb" (عالِمُ الغَيْبِ) is read by Madani and Shami readers, meaning "He is the Knower of the unseen," and "ʿAllāmi al-ghayb" (عَلّامِ الغَيْبِ), read by Hamzah and ʿAli, is in the intensive form (for emphasis).

﴿Not escapes from Him﴾, read with a kasra on the zay by ʿAli, from "ʿazaba, yaʿzibu" (عَزَبَ، يَعْزِبُ), meaning to be absent and to be far away,

﴿an atom's weight﴾, the measure of the smallest ant,

﴿in the heavens or on the earth, nor anything smaller than that﴾, than an atom's weight,

﴿nor greater﴾, than an atom's weight,

﴿but it is in a Clear Record﴾, that is, in the Preserved Tablet. "Wa lā aṣghara" (وَلا أصْغَرُ) and "wa lā akbara" (وَلا أكْبَرُ) with the nominative case are coordinated with "mithqālu dharrah" (مِثْقالُ ذَرَّةٍ), and "illā" (إلّا) would then mean "but" (lākin), or they are nominative as subjects, with the predicate being "fī kitābin" (فِي كِتابٍ).

The lam in ﴿So that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds; those—for them is forgiveness﴾ is (for the reason of) what they fell short of of the stages of faith,

﴿and a noble provision﴾ is (for the reason of) what they endured of the paths of excellence (ihsan). It is connected to "la-ta'tiyannakum" (the Hour will surely come upon you), as a causal clause (ta'lil) for it.

(p-53) ﴿Those who strive against Our signs﴾: they struggle to reject the Qur'an. ﴿Seeking to frustrate [Us]﴾: racing [against Us], thinking that they can escape Us. "Mu'ajjizin" (with shaddah on the ʿayn) is read by Makki and Abu ʿAmr, meaning: discouraging people from following it and reflecting upon it; or attributing incapacity (ʿajz) to God.

﴿For them is a painful punishment of a rijz﴾ with the mīm in the nominative (raf'), read by Makki, Hafs and Ya'qub, as an attribute of ʿadhāb, meaning: "a painful punishment of an evil torment." Qatadah said: "al-rijz" is evil torment. Others read it in the genitive (jarr), as an attribute of rijz.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 6:

﴿And they see﴾, in the place of raf' (nominative), by way of isti'naf (resumptive new sentence), i.e., "and He knows" [or: "and it is known"],

﴿those who have been given knowledge﴾, meaning the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and whoever follows in their footsteps from among his ummah, or the scholars of the People of the Book who embraced Islam, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and Kaʿb al-Ahbar,

﴿that which has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾, meaning the Qur'an,

﴿is the truth﴾, i.e., the sincere truth (al-sidq). "Huwa" is a separator (fasl, pronoun of separation), and "al-haqq" is a second object (maf'ul thani), or in the place of nasb, conjoined to "li-yajza" [so that He may recompense], i.e., "and that those of knowledge may know at the coming of the Hour that it is the truth, with a knowledge to which nothing can be added in certainty,"

﴿and guides﴾, Allah, or "that which has been sent down to you,"

﴿to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾, and this is the religion of Allah.

وَقالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا ﴿And those who disbelieved said⦆. Quraysh said to one another:

﴿هَلْ نَدُلُّكم عَلى رَجُلٍ﴾ ﴿Shall we direct you to a man⦆, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). They used the indefinite form (nakkarūhu), even though he was well known, a prominent figure among Quraysh, and his announcement of the Resurrection was widely known among them, as a form of feigned ignorance (tajāhul) concerning him and his matter. The device of feigned ignorance (bāb al-tajāhul) is among the eloquent devices in rhetoric (al-balāgha) and its magic (sihrihā).

﴿يُنَبِّئُكم إذا مُزِّقْتُمْ كُلَّ مُمَزَّقٍ إنَّكم لَفي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ﴾ ﴿He informs you, when you are completely torn apart, that you will indeed be in a new creation.⦆ That is: he tells you of a marvel among marvels, that you will be resurrected and brought forth as a new creation after you have become dust and fragments, and after decay has torn your bodies "into every tearing apart", that is, scattering you in every manner of dispersal. Thus "al-mumazzaq" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) meaning tamzīq (tearing apart). The element governing "idhā" is what is indicated by ﴿إنَّكم لَفي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ﴾, that is, "you will be resurrected". As for "al-jadīd", it is on the pattern fa‘īl, meaning fā‘il, according to the Basrans; one says "jadda, fa-huwa jadīd", like "qalla, fa-huwa qalīl". It is not permissible to read "annakum" with a fatḥa, because of the lām in its predicate.

**Qur'an 34:8: "Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?"**

﴿Has he invented against Allah a lie?﴾ Is he one who fabricates against Allah a lie concerning what is attributed to Him of such things?! The hamza (interrogative particle, *hamzat al-istifham*) is for questioning, and the hamzat al-wasl (the connecting hamza) has been dropped as being unnecessary.

﴿Or is there in him madness?﴾ *Junnah* means madness; this suggests to him (the Prophet) that such a condition, and it casts it upon his tongue.

﴿Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in punishment and far error.﴾ Then He, glorified and exalted, said: Muhammad is free of fabrication and madness in any way, and he is cleared of both. Rather, these disbelievers who deny resurrection are in the punishment of the Fire, and in the error from the truth to which it leads them, while they are heedless of it. This is the most extreme madness. Their being in punishment has been made a consequence (*rasil*) of their being in error, as though both occur at one time, because error, of which punishment is a necessary result, has been treated as though the two are joined. He described the error as "*al-ba'id*" (far), which is a metaphorical attribution (*al-isnad al-majazi*), because "far" is really a description of the one who strays when he moves away from the right path (*al-jaddah*).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 34, verse 9:

﴿Have they not looked at what is before them and behind them of the heaven and the earth? If We wish, We shall cause the earth to swallow them up,﴾ and it is also recited with assimilation (*idgham*, merging one sound into the next) because the *fa'* and the *ba'* are close in articulation. Some scholars regarded this reading as weak, because the sound of the *fa'* is more prominent than that of the *ba'*.

﴿or cause fragments of the sky to fall upon them﴾: all three verbs are read with *ya'* (as *yakhsif* and *yusqit*, third person). This is the reading of the Kufans other than ʿĀṣim (*Kūfī ghayra ʿĀṣim*), in line with the verse ﴿Has he invented a lie against God?﴾ (*aftará ʿalá Allāhi kadhiban*).

﴿kisafan﴾, read as *kisfan* by Ḥafṣ.

﴿from the sky﴾: meaning, have they been blind and not looked at the heaven and the earth, and at how they encompass them wherever they are, and in whichever direction they travel, both before them and behind them, so that they cannot pass beyond their outer limits or get out of what they are in of the dominion (*malakūt*) of God? Have they not feared that God might cause the earth to swallow them up, or cause fragments of the sky to fall upon them, because of their denial of the signs and their disbelief in the Messenger and in what he brought, just as was done to Qarun and to the People of the Thicket?

﴿Indeed in that﴾: in looking at the heaven and the earth and reflecting upon them, and in what they indicate of the power of God (Exalted),

﴿is a sign﴾: that is, a proof,

﴿for every servant who turns back in repentance﴾: who returns to his Lord and obeys Him. For the one who turns back in repentance cannot be without considering the signs of God, which show that He is capable of all things, including the resurrection and the punishment of those who disbelieve in Him.

﴿And We bestowed upon Dawud from Us a bounty: O mountains!﴾ This is a substitute (badal, apposition) for "fadlan" (a bounty), or for "ataynā" (We bestowed), with the implied phrase "qawlanā yā jibālu" (Our saying: O mountains), or "qulnā yā jibālu" (We said: O mountains).

﴿Awwibī maʿahu﴾: the imperative "awwibī" derives from al-ta'wīb (returning, repeating), meaning "return with him the glorification (al-tasbīḥ)." The meaning of the glorification of the mountains is that God creates glorification in them, so that it is heard from them as it is heard from one who glorifies, as a miracle for Dawud (peace be upon him).

﴿wal-ṭayr﴾ ("and the birds"): this is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the position (maḥall) of "al-jibāl" (the mountains), while "wal-ṭayr" is a conjunction on the wording (lafẓ) of "al-jibāl." In this arrangement there is a grandeur that is not hidden: the mountains are placed in the status of rational beings who, when commanded to obey, obey, and when called, respond. This signals that there is no living creature that is not submissive to the will of God (exalted is He). Had it said, "We bestowed upon Dawud from Us a bounty: the returning of the mountains with him and the birds," this grandeur would not have been present.

﴿And We made iron soft for him﴾: We made it pliable for him like kneaded clay, so that he shaped it with his hand as he willed, without fire and without striking with a hammer. It is also said: the iron became soft in his hand because of the great strength he had been given.

﴿That work﴾. "An" here means "i.e.", as if to say: We commanded him, "work". ﴿Full coats of mail﴾: wide, complete armor, from "sabugh" (fullness). He was the first to make them, and he would sell a coat of mail for four thousand (dirhams). He would spend from it on himself and his dependents and give charity to the poor. It was also said that he would go out in disguise and ask people about himself, saying to them, "What do you say about Dawud?" They would praise him. So God sent him an angel in human form, and he asked him, as was his habit. The angel said, "What a fine man, were it not for one trait in him: he feeds his dependents from the public treasury (bayt al-mal)." So he asked his Lord at that point to provide him with a means by which he could be independent of the public treasury, and God taught him the craft of making coats of mail. "And measure well in the weaving (al-sard)": do not make the rivets too fine, lest they split, nor too thick, lest the links break. "Al-sard" (the weaving) means the braiding of coats of mail. (p-٥٦) ﴿And work﴾: the pronoun refers to Dawud and his family.

﴿Righteous﴾: sincere, fit to be accepted.

﴿Indeed I am Seeing of what you do﴾: so I will recompense you for it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 12:

﴿And to Sulayman We subjected the wind﴾, i.e., We subjected the wind to Sulayman, and it was the easterly wind (al-Saba). Abu Bakr, Hammad and al-Fadl read "al-rih" in the nominative (al-rīḥu), i.e., "and for Sulayman the wind is subjected," (muskhkharatun).

﴿Its morning course was a month's journey and its evening course was a month's journey﴾: its course in the morning was the distance of a month's travel, and its course in the evening was likewise. He would set out in the morning from Damascus and take his midday rest at Istakhr in Persia, and the distance between them is a month's journey; and he would set out from Istakhr in the afternoon and spend the night in Kabul, and the distance between them is a month's journey for a rider who travels swiftly. It was also said: he would have his midday meal in al-Rayy and his evening meal in Samarqand.

﴿And We caused a spring of copper to flow for him﴾: i.e., a mine of copper. Al-qitr is copper, and it is also called al-sufr (brass). He caused it to flow, although it had not previously melted, and it flowed for three days a month, as water flows. Before Sulayman it did not melt, and he called it "the spring of copper" by the name of what it became.

﴿And of the jinn were those who worked before him﴾: "man" (those who) is in the accusative position, i.e., We subjected to him from among the jinn those who worked ﴿before him by the permission of his Lord﴾, by the command of his Lord.

﴿And whoever of them deviates﴾: whoever of them turns aside,

﴿from Our command﴾: that which We commanded, namely obedience to Sulayman,

﴿We will make him taste of the punishment of the Blaze﴾: the punishment of the Hereafter. It was also said: there was an angel with him holding a whip of fire, and whoever deviated from the command of Sulayman, peace be upon him, he struck with a blow that burned him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 13:

﴿They made for him whatever he willed: sanctuaries (mahārīb), that is, places of worship (masājid), or dwellings (masākin),﴾

﴿and statues (tamāthīl)﴾, that is, images of lions and birds. It is related that they made for him two lions at the base of his throne and two eagles above it. When he wished to ascend, the two lions would extend their forelegs to him, and when he sat, the two eagles would shade him with their wings. Depiction (taṣwīr) was permissible at that time.

﴿and basins (jifān)﴾, the plural of "jafna" (large basin),

﴿like reservoirs (jawāb)﴾, the plural of "jābiya" (jābiya), which are large cisterns. It is said that a thousand men could sit upon one jafna. "Kal-jawābī" (with the yāʾ), in both connected and pausal reading, is read by Makkī, Yaʿqūb and Sahl; Abū ʿAmr agreed with them in connected reading, while the rest read it without a yāʾ, relying on the kasra (as a sufficient indication).

﴿and fixed cooking pots (qudūr rāsiyāt)﴾, firmly set upon their hearths (al-athāfī), not moved from them because of their great size. It is said that they still survive in Yemen. And We said to them: ﴿Work, family of Dawud, in gratitude (shukran)﴾, that is, show mercy to the people of the lands and ask your Lord for well-being, related from al-Fudayl. "Shukran" is an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), or a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning "grateful"; or it is a absolute object ("be grateful with gratitude"), since "iʿmalū" (work) carries the sense of "ushkurū" (be grateful), inasmuch as working for the benefactor is gratitude to him; or it is a direct object, meaning: "We have subjected to you the jinn, who work for you whatever you wish; so you, work in gratitude." Al-Junayd was asked about gratitude and said: "Exerting one's utmost effort before the One worshipped."

﴿And few of My servants are grateful (qalīl min ʿibādiya al-shakūr)﴾ with the yāʾ silent, read by Ḥamza, and others read it with the yāʾ vowelled (fatḥa).

﴿al-Shakūr﴾: the one who is fully devoted to rendering gratitude, expending his utmost capacity in it, having occupied his heart, tongue and limbs with it, through belief, acknowledgment and striving. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "One who gives thanks in all his circumstances." It is also said: one who gives thanks for the very ability to give thanks; and it is said: one who sees his inability to give thanks. It is related from Dawud, peace be upon him, that he divided the hours of the night and day among his family, so that there was never an hour of the hours without a member of the family of Dawud standing in prayer.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 14:

﴿Then when We decreed death upon him﴾, that is, upon Sulayman (Solomon),

﴿nothing showed them﴾, that is, the jinn and the family of Dawud (David),

﴿his death except a creature of the earth﴾, that is, the termite (al-arada), which is a small creature called "sirfa" and "al-ard." Its action is "al-ard," and it is attributed to it [i.e., the creature is named after its action]. It is said: "The wood was eaten (uridat al-khashaba aradan)" when the termite had eaten it,

﴿eating away at his staff﴾. "Al-minsa'ah" is the staff, because one is driven away (yunsa'u) with it, that is, one is pushed away. "Minsataho" without a hamza is read by Madani and Abu 'Amr,

﴿So when he fell﴾, Sulayman fell,

﴿the jinn saw clearly﴾, all the jinn came to know clearly, after the matter had been obscured to their common folk and their weak ones,

﴿that had they known the unseen, they would not have remained﴾, after the death of Sulayman,

﴿in the humiliating punishment.﴾ It is related that Dawud, peace be upon him, laid the foundation of the building of Bayt al-Maqdis (the Holy House, Jerusalem) at the site of the tent of Musa, peace be upon him, but he died before he could complete it. He entrusted it to Sulayman, and he commanded the devils to complete it. When one year of his life remained, he asked his Lord to conceal his death from them until they finished it, and so that their claim of knowing the unseen would be proven false. Sulayman's lifespan was fifty-three years; he became king at the age of thirteen, and remained in his kingdom for forty years. He began building Bayt al-Maqdis four years into his reign. It is also related that Afridun came to climb his throne, but when he approached, the two lions struck his leg and broke it, and no one after him dared to approach it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 34, verse 15:

﴿لَقَدْ كانَ لِسَبَإٍ﴾: with *ṣarf* (tanwīn, the nunation on *Saba'*), according to the reading of the *ḥayy* (the tribe as a living group). Without it, according to Abū ʿAmr. The reading is also explained by taking *Saba'* to mean the *qabīla* (the tribe).

﴿فِي مَسْكَنِهِمْ﴾: read *maskinihim* by Ḥamzah and Ḥafṣ, and *maskanihim* by ʿAlī and Khalaf. It means the place where they dwelt, their land, and their country, in which they lived in Yemen. Or it means the dwelling of each one of them. Others read *masākinihim*.

﴿آيَةٌ﴾: the *ism* (subject) of *kāna* (the subject of the verb *kāna*, "there was").

﴿جَنَّتانِ﴾: a *badal* (appositive) of *āyah*, or the *khabar* (predicate) of an omitted *mubtada'* (subject), whose implied meaning is: "The sign is two gardens." The meaning of them being a sign is that when its people turned away from thanking God, God took away their blessing, so that they might take warning or be admonished, and not return to what they had been upon of disbelief and denial of blessings. Or He made them a sign, that is, a token, indicating God's power, His beneficence, and the obligation to thank Him.

﴿عَنْ يَمِينٍ وشِمالٍ﴾: He meant two groups of gardens: one group on the right of their town, and another on its left. Each of the two groups, because of their closeness and compactness, was like one single garden, as the gardens of well-populated towns are. Or He meant the two gardens of each man among them, on the right and left of his dwelling.

﴿كُلُوا مِن رِزْقِ رَبِّكم واشْكُرُوا لَهُ﴾: this is a report of what the prophets of God, who were sent to them, said. Or it is what the tongue of their speech said to them, or they were deserving that this be said to them. When He commanded them with this, He followed it with His saying: ﴿بَلْدَةٌ طَيِّبَةٌ ورَبٌّ غَفُورٌ﴾, that is: this town in which your provision is, is a good town, and your Lord who provided for you and asked for your thanks is a forgiving Lord to whoever thanks Him.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Saba' was three *farsakh* (leagues) from Ṣanʿāʾ, and it was the most fertile of lands. A woman would go out with a basket on her head and work with her hand, walking among those trees, and the basket would fill with the fruit that fell into it, by itself, from the trees. Its air was pure, and there were no gnats, no flies, no fleas, no scorpions, and no snakes in it. Any stranger who passed through it would have his lice die because of the purity of its air."

(p-٥٩)

﴿So they turned away﴾ from the call of their prophets, and they denied them, and said: "We do not recognise any blessing of God upon us."

﴿So We sent against them the flood of the dam (al-'Arim)﴾, that is, the heavy rain. Or "al-'Arim" is the name of a valley. Or it is the rat that gnawed through the dam for them when they transgressed. God sent the rat against them, and it gnawed through it from its base, so it drowned them.

﴿And We replaced their two gardens﴾ mentioned above,

﴿with two gardens﴾. Naming the replacement "two gardens" is for the sake of parallelism (al-mushakalah) and the harmony of the speech, as in His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

﴿Bearing bitter fruit (dhawatay ukulin khamt)﴾. "Al-ukul" means the fruit, and it may be read with a heavy or light pronunciation (of the kaf); this is the recitation (qira'ah, a canonical reading) of Nafi' and Makki. "Al-khamt" is the tamarisk tree (shajar al-arak). It was also said: every tree with thorns.

﴿And tamarisk, and a few lote-trees﴾. "Al-athl" is a tree resembling the tamarisk (al-tara'if) but larger, and of better wood. As for the one who read "al-ukul" with tanwin (nunation), other than Abu 'Amr, the justification is that its original form was "dhawatay ukulin ukli khamtin" (two gardens of fruit, the fruit of bitter fruit), so the qualifying noun was deleted and the noun in the genitive was put in its place. Or "al-ukul" was described by "khamt", as if it were said "dhawatay ukulin bashi'" (two gardens of bitter fruit). The justification of Abu 'Amr is that "ukul al-khamt" carries the meaning of al-bariri (the unripe fruit of the arak tree, when it is fresh). It is as if it were said: "two gardens of bariri". "Al-athl" and "al-sidr" are conjoined to "ukul", not to "khamt", because the athl has no edible fruit. Al-Hasan said: He made the lote-trees few because it is the most noble of what they exchanged, since it is found in the gardens (al-jinan).

ذَلِكَ جَزَيْناهم بِما كَفَرُوا ("That is how We recompensed them for their disbelief"), i.e., We repaid them that (punishment) for their kufr. Here it is the second object, placed first (fa-huwa maf'ul thani muqaddam).

﴿وَهَلْ نُجازِي إلا الكَفُورَ﴾ ("And do We recompense any but the ungrateful?"). Kufi readers other than Abu Bakr read it as "وَهَلْ نُجازِي", while others read it as "وَهَلْ يُجازى إلّا الكَفُورُ" ("and is any recompensed but the ungrateful?"). The meaning is: Do We requite such a recompense except those who denied the blessing and did not thank for it, or who disbelieved in Allah? Or: is anyone punished except them? This is because jaza' (recompense) - though general - is used both for punishment and for reward, but the intended sense here is the specific one, which is punishment (ʿiqab).

And it is reported from al-Dahhak: they lived in the fatra (the interval) between ʿIsa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 18:

﴿And We placed between them﴾, between Saba',

﴿and between the towns which We had blessed﴾, by widening (the provision) for their people in bounties and waters, and these are the towns of al-Sham (Greater Syria),

﴿visible towns﴾, consecutive, one of them visible from another because of their proximity; so they are visible to the eyes of onlookers, or visible to the travellers (al-sabila), not so far from their routes that they would be hidden from them. They were four thousand and seven hundred towns, contiguous from Saba' to al-Sham,

﴿and We apportioned therein the travel﴾, meaning: We made these towns of a known measure, such that the traveller would take his midday rest in one town and his evening rest in another, until he reached al-Sham,

﴿"Travel therein"﴾, and We said to them: "Travel," and there was no speech there, but when they were enabled to travel, and its means were made smooth for them, it was as though they were commanded to do so,

﴿"by night and by day, secure"﴾, meaning: travel in them, if you wish, by night, and if you wish, by day, for security therein does not differ with the difference of times; that is, travel in them secure, not fearing an enemy, nor hunger, nor thirst, even if the duration of your journey is prolonged and extends over nights and days.

﴿So they said, "Our Lord, make the distance between our journeys farther."﴾ They said, "Would that they had been far apart, so that we could travel on our swift camels, trade for profit, and boast about our mounts and possessions." They became insolent about the blessing and grew weary of well-being, so they sought hardship and toil. "Make it farther" (*ba'id*), is the reading of Makki (Ibn Kathir) and Abu 'Amr (ibn al-'Ala').

﴿And they wronged themselves﴾ by what they said.

﴿So We made them into tales﴾, which people narrate, marveling at their circumstances.

﴿And We scattered them completely﴾, and We dispersed them into a dispersal that people took as a proverb struck for others. They say, "They went the way of the hands of Saba'" and "They scattered like the hands of Saba'." Ghassan went to al-Sham (Syria), Anmar went to Yathrib, Judham went to Tihama, and al-Azd went to Oman.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast one﴾ who refrains from sins,

﴿grateful﴾ for blessings. Or it means every believer, because faith is of two halves: half of it is gratitude and half of it is patience.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 20:

﴿And Iblis certainly confirmed his assumption about them, so they followed him, except for a party of the believers﴾. [It is read] with the shaddah (emphatic doubling), "Kufi" (i.e., the reading of the people of Kufa), meaning: he fulfilled his assumption about them, or found it true. And with the lightening (without shaddah), the rest [of the readers], meaning: he was truthful in his assumption.

﴿So they followed him﴾. (p-61) The pronoun in "ʿalayhim" ("about them") and "ittabaʿūhu" ("they followed him") refers to the people of Sheba (Saba'), or to the children of Adam. He made the believers few by His saying: ﴿except for a party of the believers﴾, because of their paucity in comparison with the disbelievers. And [He says]: ﴿and you will not find most of them grateful﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 21:

﴿And he had no authority over them﴾: that is, Iblis had no authority over those about whom his assumption proved true,

﴿except that We might make evident﴾: that is, through domination and taking control by means of whispering,

﴿[He had no authority over them] except that We might know﴾: that is, [We might know] as existing what We already knew as non-existent. The change occurs in the object of knowledge, not in the knowledge itself.

﴿who believes in the Hereafter from one who is in doubt about it. And your Lord is Guardian over all things﴾: that is, Protector over it. "Fa'il" and "mufa'il" are interchangeable in meaning.

﴿Say﴾, (to) the polytheists of your people:

﴿Call upon those whom you claimed﴾ besides Allah, meaning: whom you claimed to be gods besides Allah. So the first object of *zaʿamtum* (you claimed) is the pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*, "those whom"). It was omitted, as it was omitted in His saying ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?﴾, for brevity, because the relative clause is long with its complement (*al-ṣila*, the clause that completes the relative pronoun). The second object is *ālihatan* (gods), and it was omitted because it is a modified noun (*mawṣūf*) whose qualifier (*ṣifa*) is ﴿besides Allah﴾. It is permissible to omit the modified noun and let the qualifier stand in its place when it is understood. Thus both objects of *zaʿama* are omitted, for two different reasons. The meaning is: "Call upon those whom you worshipped besides Allah, among the idols and the angels, and whom you named (as gods), and turn to them in what afflicts you, as you turn to Him, and await their response to your call, as you await His response." Then He answered them by saying:

﴿They do not possess an atom's weight﴾ of good or evil, benefit or harm,

﴿in the heavens or on the earth, nor do they have in them any share﴾ of creation or dominion in these two realms.

﴿And He has not﴾ (Exalted is He)

﴿among them﴾, that is, among their gods,

﴿any helper﴾, that is, any assistant who helps Him in the management of His creation. He means that they have this attribute of incapacity, so how could it be right for them to be called upon as He is called upon, and hoped in as He is hoped in?!

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 23:

﴿And intercession with Him does not benefit except for one whom He has permitted.﴾ That is: whom Allah has permitted, meaning, except for the one for whom permission has been granted to the intercessor, and this is the second lam in your saying, "Permission was granted to Zayd for ʿAmr," meaning: for his sake. This is a refutation of their saying, "These are our intercessors with Allah." "Permitted for him," "Kufan other than ʿĀṣim," except al-Aʿshā,

﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾ That is: the fear is uncovered from the hearts of the intercessors and those for whom intercession is sought, by a word spoken by the Lord of Majesty in releasing the permission. "Fazzaʿa" (with the verb in the passive, "was removed") is Shamī's reading, meaning Allah (Exalted is He). "At-Tafzīʿ" is the removal of fear. "Ḥattā" (until) marks the limit of what is understood from the fact that there is waiting for permission, hesitation, and fear among those who hope for intercession and among the intercessors, as to whether they will be permitted or not. It is as if it were said: they wait and anticipate for a long time, in fear.

﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts, they say﴾, some of them asking others: ﴿"What has your Lord said?"﴾ They say: ﴿"The truth,"﴾ that is, the word of truth, which is the permission for intercession for whomever He approves.

﴿And He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾, possessor of exaltedness and greatness. No angel or prophet may speak on that Day except by His permission, and none may intercede except for one whom He approves.

﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?﴾ Say: ﴿Allah.﴾ He commanded him to establish their acknowledgment by saying, "Who provides for you?" Then he commanded him to take on the answer and the affirmation on their behalf by saying, "Allah provides for you." This indicates that they affirm it in their hearts, though they may refuse to say it with their tongues. For if they were to utter that Allah is their provider, it would be incumbent upon them to be told: "Why then do you not worship the One who provides for you, and prefer over Him one who has no power over provision?" He commanded him to say to them, after the binding argument and the silencing, which adds nothing to their confession with their tongues but is not less than it: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error.﴾ Its meaning: indeed one of the two groups, the monotheists or the polytheists, is surely upon one of the two states, guidance or error. This is from fair speech (min al-kalam al-munsif), such that whoever hears it, whether a friend or a hypocrite, says to the one addressed by it: "Your companion has been fair with you." Within its arrangement, after the preceding affirmation, there is a clear indication of which of the two groups is upon guidance and which is in clear error. But allusion (al-ta'rid, indirect reference) brings the debater closer to the aim, and similar to it is your saying to the liar: "Indeed one of us is a liar." The two prepositions that govern guidance and error were varied, because the possessor of guidance is as if he were mounted on a swift steed, driving it wherever he wishes, while the one who is astray is as if he were plunged into darkness, not knowing where to turn.

Qur'anic quotation: "Say: You will not be asked about what we have committed as criminals, nor will we be asked about what you do."

This is more equitable (adkhalu fi al-insaf) than the first, in that it attributes the crime (al-ijram) to the addressees, though it is something from which one is restrained and forbidden, and it attributes the act (al-'amal) to the addressees, though it is something commanded and praiseworthy.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 26:

﴿Say: Our Lord will gather us together﴾, on the Day of Resurrection,

﴿then He will decide﴾, He will judge,

﴿between us with truth﴾, without injustice or partiality,

﴿and He is the Opener﴾, the Judge,

﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of the judgment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 27:

﴿Say: Show me those whom you have joined with Him﴾, i.e., whom you have joined to Him,

﴿as partners﴾ (شُرَكاءَ), in worship alongside Him. The meaning of His saying "﴿Show me﴾" – though He sees them – is that He may show them the great error in attributing partners to Allah, and inform them of the state of associating others with Him.

﴿Nay﴾ (كَلا), is a rebuke and a warning, i.e., desist from this statement and become aware of your misguidance.

﴿Rather, He is Allah, the Mighty﴾ (العَزِيزُ), the Victorious, so no one shares with Him, and "He" (هُوَ) is the pronoun of the matter (ضَمِيرُ الشَأْنِ),

﴿the Wise﴾ (الحَكِيمُ), in His management.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 28:

﴿And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind﴾, except as a general message to them, encompassing them, for when it encompasses them, it has restrained them from any of them going outside it. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of "kaffa" (comprehensive, all-inclusive) in the language is "al-ihata" (encompassing), and the meaning is: "We have sent you gathering mankind in warning and conveying (the message)." So he made it a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the kaf and the ta' according to this, for emphasis, like the ta' in "al-rawiya" (the great transmitter) and "al-allama" (the very learned one).

﴿Bashiran﴾ (a bringer of good tidings), with bounty, for whoever affirms (the truth),

﴿wa-nadhiran﴾ (and a warner), with justice, for whoever persists (in denial).

﴿Wa-lakinna akthar al-nasi la ya'lamun﴾ (But most people do not know), so their ignorance drives them to oppose you.

"And they say: When is this promise (fulfilled), if you are truthful?" That is: the Resurrection (al-qiyamah), which was alluded to in His saying: "Say: Our Lord will gather us together."

﴿If you are truthful﴾

"Say: 'For you is the appointed time of a Day'" (﴿قُلْ لَكم مِيعادُ يَوْمٍ﴾). Al-mi'ad (the appointed time, appointment) is the noun of place or time of the promise (waʿd), whether of a place or a time; here it refers to time. This is shown by the reading of one who recited "mi'ad yawm" (مِيعادٌ يَوْمٌ) with the nominative, making "yawm" a substitute (badal) for it. As for the construction (idafah) here, it is an idafah of explanation (idafat al-tabyin), as when you say "ba'ir saniyah" (بَعِيرُ سانِيَةٍ) (a camel that draws water).

"You cannot delay from it by an hour, nor advance" (﴿لا تَسْتَأْخِرُونَ عَنْهُ ساعَةً ولا تَسْتَقْدِمُونَ﴾). That is: it is not possible for you to postpone it by asking for respite, nor to bring it forward by seeking haste. The way this answer corresponds to their question is that they asked about it while denying it, out of obstinacy and not out of seeking guidance. So the answer came in the form of a threat, matching the question in its denial and obstinacy, and informing them that they are awaited by a Day that will surprise them, so they will not be able to delay from it or advance before it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 31:

﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, i.e., Abu Jahl and his kind,

﴿"We will never believe in this Qur'an or in that which came before it"﴾, i.e., what was revealed before the Qur'an of the Books of Allah, or the Resurrection, the Garden and the Fire, to the extent that they denied that the Qur'an is from Allah, and that it indicates the return (al-i'adah) in truth,

﴿And if you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord﴾, detained,

﴿returning the word (yarji'u ba'duhum ila ba'din al-qawl) to one another﴾, i.e., they cast it back, in the argument. He informed about the outcome of their affair and their end in the Hereafter, and so he said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, or to the one addressed: "And if you could see in the Hereafter their station, as they toss between them the ends of the dispute and send them back to one another, you would see a marvel," and so the answer was omitted,

﴿Those who were oppressed will say﴾, i.e., the followers,

﴿to those who were arrogant﴾, i.e., to the leaders and the foremost,

﴿"Had it not been for you, we would have been believers"﴾, had it not been for your calling us to disbelief, we would have been believers in Allah and His Messenger.

(p-65) ﴿They who were arrogant said to those who were deemed weak: "Is it we who barred you from guidance?"﴾ The word "we" (أنحن, anaḥnu) was given the interrogative particle of denial (ḥarf al-inkār), because the intended meaning is a denial that they were the ones who barred them from faith, and an affirmation that they themselves were the ones who turned away from it on their own, and that they were stricken (أُوتُوا) from their own side, by their own choice.

﴿after there had come to you﴾: "idh" (إذ) came to be used as a noun governed by a preposition (مضافًا إليها, i.e., governing what follows as its genitive complement). Although "idh" and "idhā" (إذا) are among the adverbs that necessarily function as adverbs of time (ẓurūf lāzimah li-l-ẓarfiyyah), time has been extended in usage to a degree it has not been extended in other cases, so time was made to be governed by them.

﴿Rather, you were criminals﴾: that is, disbelievers, by your own choice and your preference of misguidance over guidance, not by our saying or our enticing.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 33:

﴿And those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant﴾. He did not use the conjunctive particle (al-'atif) in "Those who were arrogant said," but he used it in "And those who were oppressed said," because the speech of those who were oppressed came first, so the reply was given without the conjunctive particle, by way of istinaf (resumption, a new sentence), and then another statement was made by the oppressed, so it was conjoined to their first statement.

﴿Nay, it is the plotting of the night and the day﴾. Rather, your plotting against us by night and by day. The adverb of time (zarf) is extended by treating it as the object (maf'ul bihi) and by attributing the plotting to it, or by making their night and day the ones who plot, by way of metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), meaning: "The night and the day plotted, by the long continuance of safety in them, until we thought that you were upon the truth."

﴿When you used to command us to disbelieve in Allah and set up rivals to Him﴾, i.e., equals (ashbahan). The meaning is that when the arrogant denied, by their saying, "Did we turn you away?", that they were the cause of the disbelief of the oppressed, and affirmed, by their saying, "Rather, you were criminals," that this was by your own earning and choice, the oppressed turned back upon them with their saying, ﴿Nay, it is the plotting of the night and the day﴾, thereby nullifying their denial by a denial of their own. It is as if they said: "The crime did not come from our side; rather, it came from your plotting against us, unceasingly, by night and by day, or from your compelling us to associate partners with Allah and to take rivals."

﴿And they will conceal their regret﴾. (Asarru) means they concealed it or they displayed it; it is one of the words with contrary meanings (al-adda'). And they are the wrongdoers, in His saying: ﴿When the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord﴾ [Saba': 31]. The arrogant regret their misguidance and their misguiding of others, and the oppressed regret their misguidance and their following of those who led them astray. ﴿When they see the punishment﴾, the Blazing Fire, (p-66) ﴿And We will place shackles upon the necks of those who disbelieved﴾, i.e., upon their necks. He used the explicit term to indicate what made them deserve the shackles.

﴿Will they be recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾ In this world.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 34:

﴿Never did We send a warner to any town but its affluent ones said: "Surely we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent."﴾ (a warner: a prophet)

"Its affluent ones" (mutrafuha): those who lived in luxury and comfort, and its leaders.

﴿Surely we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent.﴾ This is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ) for what he suffered from his people of denial and disbelief in what he brought. It means that no warner was ever sent to the people of any town but they said to him the same as the people of Makkah said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they boasted of their abundance of wealth and children, as He says:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 35:

﴿And they say, "We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished."﴾ They meant that they were too honored in the sight of Allah for Him to punish them, judging by their circumstances in this world. They thought that if they were not honored by Allah, He would not have provided for them, and that were it not for the believers being humiliated before Him, He would not have deprived them. So Allah nullified their assumption that provision is a favor from Allah, which He distributes however He wills. Thus He may expand provision for the disobedient and restrict it for the obedient, He may reverse this, or He may expand it for both or restrict it for both. Therefore, the matter of reward cannot be inferred from these (worldly circumstances). And that is His saying:

﴿Say: Indeed my Lord extends provision to whomever He wills, and restricts it.﴾ The measure of provision (qadr al-rizq) is its restriction (tadyiq). God (Exalted is He) says: ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted﴾ [al-Talaq: 7]. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ that.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 37:

﴿And it is not your wealth nor your children that will bring you near to Us in nearness﴾. That is: it is not the multitude of your wealth, nor the multitude of your children, that will bring you near. This is because the broken plural (jam' al-taksir, the plural pattern that breaks the singular form) treats rational and non-rational referents alike in terms of feminine agreement. "Al-zulfa" and "al-zulfah" are like "al-qurba" and "al-qurbah." Its position is accusative, as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: it brings you near as a nearness (qurbah), like His saying: ﴿And He caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17]. ﴿Except for one who believes and does righteous work﴾: the exception is from "kum" in "tuqarribukum" (you), meaning that wealth does not bring anyone near except the believing righteous person who spends it in the way of Allah, and children do not bring anyone near except one who teaches them good, gives them understanding of the religion, and guides them to righteousness and obedience. It is also reported from Ibn 'Isa that "illa" (except) here carries the sense of "lakin" (but), and "man" (whoever) is a conditional particle whose answer is: ﴿then those will have the recompense of double for what they have done﴾. This is an idafah (genitive construction) of the verbal noun to its object; its original form is: "fa-ula'ika lahum an yujazaw al-di'f" (then for those is that they be recompensed the double), then "jaza' al-di'f," then "jaza'u al-di'f." The meaning of "jaza'u al-di'f" is that each of their good deeds is multiplied tenfold for them. Ya'qub read "jaza'an al-di'fu," as in "fa-ula'ika lahumu al-di'fu jaza'an" (then for those the double is the recompense).

﴿for what they did﴾: for their deeds.

﴿And they will be in the lofty chambers﴾, that is, in the chambers of the dwellings of Paradise. "Fi al-ghurfah" is read by Hamzah.

﴿secure﴾: from every frightening and distracting thing.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 38:

﴿And those who strive against Our signs﴾, to nullify them,

﴿seeking to frustrate [Our signs], those—they will be brought forth into the punishment.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 39:

﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord expands the provision﴾ (yuwassi'u, He widens it),

﴿for whomever He wills of His servants, and restricts it for him. And whatever you spend﴾ "mā" is conditional (shartiyya), in a position of accusative (naṣb),

﴿of anything﴾ is its explanation (bayānuhu),

﴿then He replaces it﴾ (yu'awwiḍuhu), there is no one else who replaces it, either swiftly with wealth or deferred with reward. It is the answer of the conditional (jawāb al-sharṭ),

﴿and He is the best of providers﴾ (al-muṭ'imīn, the feeders). This is because whatever provision others give, whether a ruler, a master, or others, is from the provision of God, who has made it flow through the hands of these people. He is the Creator of provision and the Creator of the means by which the one provided benefits from the provision. It is related from some of them: "Praise be to God who brought me into existence and made me one who desires. For how many a desirer does not find, and how many a finder does not desire."

(p-68) "And on the Day We gather them all together, then We will say to the angels: 'Did these worship you?'" — with the yā' (ي) in both places, read by Ḥafṣ and Yaʿqūb. This is an address to the angels and a rebuke to the disbelievers, coming in the manner of the proverb: "It is you I mean, but listen, O neighbour" (إيّاكِ أعْنِي واسْمَعِي يا جارَةُ).

Its like is the verse: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], and so on.

The angels said: "Glory be to You" (tanzihan laka an yu'bada ma'aka ghayruka), meaning: exalted are You above having anyone else worshipped alongside You.

"You are our Protector" (anta waliyyuna). Muwalat (taking as a close ally) is the opposite of mu'adat (hostility). It is a form of mufa'ala derived from al-walyu, which means nearness, and al-waliyy applies both to the one who gives allegiance and to the one to whom allegiance is given. The meaning is: "You are the One to whom we give our allegiance."

"Besides them" (min dunihim): since there is no alliance between us and them, the angels, by affirming their allegiance to God and their enmity toward the disbelievers, declared their disavowal of approval of being worshipped by them, because one who has this quality cannot have a state that contradicts it.

"Rather, they used to worship the jinn" (bal kanu ya'buduna al-jinn), i.e., the devils (al-shayatin), in that they obeyed them in worshipping other than God. Or they used to enter the bellies of the idols when these were worshipped, so they were worshipped through their worship. Or the devils showed them the image of a group of jinn and said: "These are the images of the angels, so worship them."

"Most of them" (aktharuhum), i.e., most of mankind, or the disbelievers.

"In them" (bihim), i.e., in the jinn.

"Believers" (mu'minun).

﴿So today none of you will possess benefit or harm for another﴾, because the command on that Day belongs to Allah alone. No one possesses in it any benefit or any harm for anyone, because the abode is the abode of reward and punishment, and the one who rewards and the one who punishes is Allah. Its state is therefore the opposite of the state of this world, which is the abode of *taklif* (legal and moral obligation), where people are left to themselves, harming and benefiting one another. The meaning is that on that Day there is no one who harms or benefits except Him. (p-69) Then he mentioned the end of the wrongdoers with His words: ﴿And We will say to those who did wrong﴾, [wrong] by placing worship in other than its proper place. This is coordinated with "does not possess":

﴿Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny﴾, in the world.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 43:

﴿When Our clear signs are recited to them﴾, i.e., when the Qur'an is recited to them,

﴿clear﴾, plain,

﴿they say﴾, i.e., the polytheists,

﴿"This is not"﴾, i.e., Muhammad,

﴿"but a man who wants to turn you away from what your forefathers used to worship." And they say, "This is not"﴾, i.e., the Qur'an,

﴿"but a fabricated lie." And those who disbelieve say﴾, i.e., they said - and the shift away from naming them is a sign of great denial and intense anger - ﴿of the truth﴾, of the Qur'an, or of the whole matter of prophethood,

﴿when it has come to them﴾, and they were unable to produce anything like it,

﴿"This is not"﴾, i.e., the truth,

﴿"but манифест sorcery"﴾, they pronounced it sorcery, then they pronounced it to be evidently clear and manifest; every intelligent person who reflected on it named it sorcery.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 44:

﴿And We did not give them any books which they could study﴾, i.e., We did not give the polytheists of Makkah books that they study, in which there is proof for the validity of polytheism,

﴿and We did not send to them before you any warner﴾, nor did We send to them a warner who would warn them of punishment if they did not associate partners with Allah. Then He threatened them for their denial with His words:

﴿And those before them denied﴾, that is: those who preceded them, from the earlier nations and the bygone generations, denied the Messengers, just as these (Makkans) have denied.

﴿And they did not reach a tenth of what We had given them﴾, that is: the people of Makkah did not reach a tenth of what the former peoples were given of long lifespans, physical strength, and abundance of wealth and children.

﴿So they denied My Messengers, so how was My rejection﴾: the word "نَكِيرِ" is read with a yā’ in both pause and continuation by Ya‘qub. This is directed at the earlier deniers, so that these (Makkans) should beware of the like of it. That is: when they denied their Messengers, My rejection came upon them in the form of destruction and annihilation, and their reliance on what they relied upon did not avail them. So what is the matter with these people?! He said "فَكَذَّبُوا" although it is dispensed with by His saying "﴿And those before them denied﴾", because when the meaning of "﴿And those before them denied﴾" was "those before them performed denial and undertook it", He made the denial of the Messengers a consequence of it. This is like the saying of one who says: "So-and-so undertook disbelief, so he disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 34, verse 46:

﴿Say, "I only admonish you with one thing"﴾, meaning one characteristic. He explained it with His saying: ﴿that you stand up﴾, taking it as an explicative apposition (*ʿaṭf bayān*, a noun that clarifies the preceding noun) for it. It was also said that it is a substitute (*badal*) construction. On these two readings, it is in the genitive position (*maḥall al-jarr*). It was also said that it is in the nominative position (*maḥall al-rafʿ*), with the implied meaning "and it is that you stand up." The accusative reading is with the implied meaning "I mean." By their standing he means rising from the gathering of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and dispersing from their assembly before him, or the standing of intent toward a matter, not rising up and getting to one's feet. The meaning is: "I only admonish you with one thing. If you do it, you will hit upon the truth and be saved. It is: that you stand ﴿for Allah﴾, that is, for the sake of Allah's face, sincerely, not out of partisanship or tribal zeal, but in pursuit of the truth."

﴿In pairs﴾: two by two.

﴿And individually﴾: one by one.

﴿Then reflect﴾: upon the matter of Muhammad ﷺ and what he brought. As for the two, they reflect together, each one presenting the product of his thinking to his companion, and they examine it with the honesty and fairness of those seeking the truth, until correct examination brings them both to the truth. Likewise, the individual reflects within himself with justice and equity, and presents his thought to his intellect. The meaning of their dispersing "in pairs and individually" is that gathering confuses thoughts, blinds insight, and prevents seeing clearly. In it fairness diminishes, injustice increases, the dust-cloud of partisanship rises, and nothing is heard but support for one's school. The word "reflect" (*tatafakkarū*) is conjoined (*maʿṭūf*) to "stand up" (*taqūmū*).

﴿Your companion﴾: meaning Muhammad ﷺ.

﴿Has any madness﴾: insanity. The meaning is: "Then reflect, so that you will know that your companion has no madness."

﴿He is not but a warner to you before a severe punishment﴾: before a severe punishment, which is the punishment of the Hereafter. This is like his ﷺ saying: "I was sent just before the Hour." (p-71)

Then he clarified that he does not seek any reward for the warning, by His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 47:

﴿Say: "Whatever reward I have asked of you﴾, for my warning and my conveying of the message,

﴿then it is yours﴾. This is the answer (jaza') to the conditional (shart). Its implied sense is: "Whatever reward I have asked of you," like His saying: ﴿Whatever mercy Allah grants to people﴾ [Fatir: 2]. Its meaning is the outright negation of asking for any reward, similar to saying: "Whatever I have in this, it is yours," meaning: "There is nothing of mine in it."

﴿Indeed my reward﴾: Madani, Shami, Abu Bakr and Hafs read it (with the yā' as a long vowel, ʾajriya), while others read it with the yā' silent (ʾajrī).

﴿is only from Allah, and He is Witness over all things﴾, so He knows that I do not seek any reward for my advice and my calling you to Him, except from Him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 48:

﴿Say: Indeed, My Lord hurls the truth﴾, by means of the revelation. Al-qadhf (the act of hurling): directing an arrow or the like with force and firm aim. It is used metaphorically for the sense of casting down, and from it is: ﴿And He cast terror into their hearts﴾ [al-Ahzab: 26], ﴿Cast him into the chest﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39]. The meaning of "yaqdhifu bil-haqq" is: He casts it down and sends it down to His prophets, or He hurls the truth at falsehood so that it crushes it and destroys it.

﴿the Knower of the unseen﴾ is in the nominative case as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "yaqdhifu", or as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada').

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 49:

﴿Say: The truth has come﴾, that is, Islam and the Qur'an.

﴿And falsehood can neither originate nor restore﴾, meaning: falsehood has vanished and perished. This is because origination (ibda') and restoration (i'ada) are attributes of a living being, so their non-existence is an expression for perishing. The meaning is: "The truth has come and falsehood has vanished," like His saying: ﴿The truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed falsehood is ever bound to vanish﴾ [al-Isra: 81]. "It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him): The Prophet (ﷺ) entered Makkah, and around the Ka'bah there were idols, so he began to strike them with a stick of nabi wood, saying: 'The truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed falsehood is ever bound to vanish. The truth has come, and falsehood can neither originate nor restore.'"

It has been said that "falsehood" (al-batil) refers to the idols. It has also been said that it refers to Iblis, because he is the possessor of falsehood, or because he is doomed to perish, just as he is called "al-Shaytan," derived from "shata," meaning he perished. That is, neither Satan nor the idol creates anyone or resurrects anyone; rather, the Originator and the Resurrector is Allah.

(p-72) When they said, "You have gone astray by abandoning the religion of your fathers," God (Exalted is He) said: ﴿Say: If I go astray﴾ from the truth,

﴿then I only go astray to my own detriment﴾. If I go astray, it is from me and upon me,

﴿and if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me﴾, i.e., by His making me firm through the revelation sent to me. The standard form of antithesis would have been: "And if I am guided, then I am guided only for it (my own benefit)," like His saying: ﴿Whoever is guided, it is for his own self, and whoever goes astray, it is only to its detriment﴾ [al-Zumar: 41]. But the two are opposite in meaning, because the self is everything that is upon it and harmful to it, so it is from it and by its cause, since it is the one that commands to evil; and what is for it, of what benefits it, is by the guidance and success of its Lord. This is a general ruling for every responsible person. He commanded His Messenger to attribute the error to himself only because when the Messenger is included in this, despite the greatness of his position and the soundness of his way, others are even more deserving of it.

﴿Indeed, He is Hearing﴾ of what I say to you,

﴿Near﴾ to me and to you; He will reward me and He will reward you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 51:

﴿And if you could see﴾, its response (jawab) is omitted, meaning: "you would see a great matter and a terrifying state,"

﴿when they are seized with terror﴾, at the Resurrection (ba'th), or at death, or on the Day of Badr,

﴿then there is no escape﴾, no place of flight, or they will not escape from Allah nor outstrip Him,

﴿and they will be seized﴾, conjoined to "they were seized with terror," meaning: "they were seized with terror and were seized, so there is no escape for them," or conjoined to "escape," in the sense: "when they were seized with terror, they did not escape, and they were seized,"

﴿from a near place﴾, from the place of standing to the Fire, when they are resurrected, or from the surface of the earth to its interior, when they die, or from the desert of Badr to the well (qalib).

"And they will say," when they witness the punishment,

"We believe in Him," meaning in Muhammad (ﷺ), because his mention had come up in the words "Your companion is not possessed" (Qur'an 34:46); or [it means] in Allah.

"But how can they reach [faith] from a distant place?" Al-tanawush (reaching, grasping) means al-tanawul (taking hold of); that is, how can they take hold of repentance when it is far from them? The meaning is that repentance was accepted from them in this world, but the world has gone and they are far from the Hereafter. It is also said that this is a parable for their seeking what cannot happen, namely that their faith would benefit them at that time as it benefited the believers in this world. Their condition is likened to that of one who wants to grasp something from a far distance (ghalwah, the range of a bowshot), just as one grasps something from the length of an arm (qays dhira').

"Al-tanaʼush" with a hamza: Abu 'Amr and the Kufans other than Hafs read it this way. The waw was made into a hamza because every waw that is pronounced with a required (lazimah) damma may be replaced by a hamza if you wish, and if you wish you need not replace it, as in your saying "adwur" and "tiqawum." If you wish you may say "ad'ur" and "taqa'um." And from Tha'lab: "al-tanaʼush," with a hamza, means taking hold from a distance; and without a hamza, taking hold from nearby.

And they had disbelieved in it before, and they hurled [assumptions] about the unseen from a distant place.

﴿And they had disbelieved in it before﴾: before the punishment, or in the world.

﴿And they hurled about the unseen﴾: this is coordinated with "they disbelieved" and narrates a past state. The meaning is that they used to speak of the unseen, or of the absent thing, saying: "There is no resurrection, no reckoning, no Paradise, and no Fire."

﴿from a distant place﴾: far from the truth, from what is right and correct. Or it refers to their saying about the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "poet, sorcerer, liar." This is speech about the unseen and the hidden matter, since they had not witnessed from him any sorcery, poetry, or lying. They brought this unseen claim from a far-off aspect of his condition, because the thing most distant from what he brought is sorcery and poetry, and the thing most distant from his known custom among them, which had been tested, is lying.

"وَيُقْذَفُونَ" (wa-yuqadhūna, "and they are hurled"), read in the passive voice according to Mahbub from Abu ʿAmr, means: their devils bring it to them and instruct them in it. If you wish, attach it to his saying "and they said: We believe in it" (Saba 52), on the basis that they are like those who seek to obtain what they neglected of faith in the world by saying "We believe" in the Hereafter. That is a demand far-fetched for one who hurls something from a distant place, where there is no room to suppose he will reach it where he wishes to fall upon it, being absent from it and far away.

It may also be that the pronoun in "amanna bihi" (we believed in it) refers to the severe punishment in his saying "before a severe punishment" (Saba 46). They used to say: "We will not be punished, if the matter is as you describe, of the rising of the Hour and of punishment and reward, and we are too honored with God for Him to punish us," analogizing the affair of the Hereafter to the affair of this world. So this was their hurling about the unseen. It is unseen, and it is hurled from a distant place, because the abode of recompense is not to be measured by the abode of obligation.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 54:**

﴿And they were barred﴾, and hindered,

﴿from what they desire﴾, namely the benefit of faith on that day, deliverance from the Fire, triumph with Paradise, or being returned to the world, as He related of them in His saying: ﴿Bring us out, that we may act righteously﴾ [Fatir: 37]. The verbs *fazi'u* (﴿they were terrified﴾), *ukhidhu* (﴿they were seized﴾), and *huyila* (﴿was barred﴾) are all in the past tense (*al-madi*), but what is meant by them is the future, because its occurrence is certain.

﴿As was done to their likes before﴾, with their counterparts among the disbelievers.

﴿Indeed they were in doubt﴾ about the matter of the Messengers and the Resurrection,

﴿disquieting﴾, causing unease, from *arabahu*, meaning he caused him to fall into *rayb* (doubt, unease). This is a refutation of those who claim that Allah does not punish for doubt (*shakk*).
